deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematical derivations. It is a set of methodological and philosophical notes, continuing the previous page's discussion of the 'naive, formal, critical' periods of mathematics and of how mathematician and physicist differ. Read in order:

(a) A quotation of Kronecker: 'Die ganzen Zahlen hat der liebe Gott gemacht, alles andere ist Menschenwerk' (God made the integers; everything else is the work of man).

(b) The main thesis: when one sets up axioms, the constants of physics make no essential difference between physical axioms and geometric axioms. Two reasons are given.

Reason 1: every constant can be approximated arbitrarily well by rationals. A rational p/q can always be described by repeating elementary operations (p-fold addition, q-fold division), so it stays within the 'integer' or arithmetical world in Kronecker's sense. Hilbert's example is Newton's law F = G m1 m2 / r^2. Stripped of the numerical value of G, it says only that F(2r) = F(r)/4 and F(3r) = F(r)/9. In general F(nr)/F(r) = 1/n^2 (this generalisation is mine). These are purely combinatorial or arithmetical relations between repeated distances.

Reason 2: constants can always be eliminated altogether. Synthetic (projective) geometry does exactly this when it sets up the 'Perspectivsatz', presumably Desargues' theorem on perspective triangles. Such an incidence theorem replaces numerical or metric data, and lets one introduce coordinates (a number system) purely geometrically. My reading: this is the idea later used in von Staudt's 'Wurfrechnung' and in the segment arithmetic of Hilbert's own Grundlagen der Geometrie (1899). Hilbert adds that it is nevertheless better to keep the constants.

(c) A start of a further contrast: there is still a real difference between the mathematician and the physicist, or practitioner generally. The mathematician needs as the object of his 'ordering', i.e. of his investigation, only... The sentence continues on the next page, which speaks of the commonly accessible notions number and circle.

Nothing is computed. The only quantitative content is the inverse-square example.
errors: No mathematical errors. The inverse-square example (1/4 at double distance, 1/9 at triple distance) is correct.

The claim that constants can 'always' be eliminated, as synthetic geometry does via the Perspectivsatz, is a programmatic assertion without justification. The analogy between eliminating physical constants and coordinatising projective geometry through Desargues' theorem is suggestive, not a proof.

results.what: Kronecker's dictum that God made the integers and all else is the work of man
results.usually_credited_to: Leopold Kronecker (said 1886 at the Berlin Naturforscherversammlung; printed in H. Weber's 1893 obituary)

results.what: Physical axioms do not differ in principle from geometric axioms, because constants can be rationally approximated or eliminated
results.modern_name: Programme of axiomatizing physics on the model of geometry (cf. Hilbert's 6th Problem, 1900)
results.usually_credited_to: David Hilbert (6th Problem 1900; lectures from the 1890s onward). Early notebook entries of this kind have been discussed by L. Corry

results.what: Elimination of numerical constants in synthetic geometry via the perspective theorem (presumably Desargues)
results.modern_name: Coordinatization of projective planes via Desargues' theorem (von Staudt's Wurfrechnung; Hilbert's Streckenrechnung)
results.usually_credited_to: von Staudt (1847–60); Hilbert, Grundlagen der Geometrie (1899)

results.what: Newton's law described as pure ratios: double distance gives 1/4 of the attraction, triple distance gives 1/9

deep.surprise_reason: These are early, pre-1900 methodological notes. They anticipate Hilbert's later programme of axiomatizing physics in parallel with geometry, and his use of Desargues-type theorems to eliminate numerical data. Both are known Hilbert themes, and such notebook entries have already been studied (Corry, Rowe). The Kronecker quote is well known. This is mildly interesting as early documentation, not a new result.

checkable.asserts: Doubling the distance reduces Newtonian attraction to one quarter
Tripling the distance reduces attraction to one ninth
General form: F(nr)/F(r) = 1/n^2, independent of the constant G
A physical constant (here G) can be represented by a rational number to any given precision
